claim: Becker muscular dystrophy (BMD) is an X-linked muscular dystrophy mostly caused by an in-frame deletion of Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD).
source: Becker muscular dystrophy (BMD), an X-linked muscular dystrophy, is mostly caused by an in-frame deletion of Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about BMD etiology.

claim: BMD severity varies from asymptomatic to severe and is associated with the genotype of DMD.
source: BMD severity varies from asymptomatic to severe, associated with the genotype of DMD.
evidence: This is established knowledge about BMD clinical heterogeneity.

claim: Three BMD mouse models were established carrying exon deletions ex45–48 del., ex45–47 del., and ex45–49 del.
source: We established BMD mice carrying three representative exon deletions: ex45–48 del., ex45–47 del., and ex45–49 del. (d45–48, d45–47, and d45–49), with high frequencies and different severities in the human BMD hotspot.
evidence: The establishment of these mouse models is described in the methods and results sections with supporting data.

claim: All three BMD mice showed muscle weakness, muscle degeneration, and fibrosis.
source: All three BMD mice showed muscle weakness, muscle degeneration, and fibrosis, but these changes appeared at different times for each exon deletion, consistent with the severities obtained by the natural history study of BMD.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from grip strength tests, histological analysis, and Sirius Red staining shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: The pathological changes in BMD mice appeared at different times for each exon deletion, consistent with the severities obtained by the natural history study of BMD.
source: All three BMD mice showed muscle weakness, muscle degeneration, and fibrosis, but these changes appeared at different times for each exon deletion, consistent with the severities obtained by the natural history study of BMD.
evidence: This is supported by time-course data in Figures 1 and 2 and comparison with human BMD natural history studies.

claim: BMD mice showed site-specific muscle changes, unlike mdx mice which showed diffuse muscle changes.
source: BMD mice showed site-specific muscle changes, unlike mdx mice, which showed diffuse muscle changes, and we demonstrated selective type IIa fiber reduction in BMD mice.
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis of different muscle regions shown in Figure 4.

claim: BMD mice demonstrated selective type IIa fiber reduction.
source: BMD mice showed site-specific muscle changes, unlike mdx mice, which showed diffuse muscle changes, and we demonstrated selective type IIa fiber reduction in BMD mice.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data for muscle fiber types shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: BMD mice showed sarcolemmal neuronal nitric oxide synthase (nNOS) reduction.
source: Furthermore, BMD mice showed sarcolemmal neuronal nitric oxide synthase (nNOS) reduction and morphological capillary changes around type IIa fibers.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry and Western blot data shown in Figure 3.

claim: BMD mice showed morphological capillary changes around type IIa fibers.
source: Furthermore, BMD mice showed sarcolemmal neuronal nitric oxide synthase (nNOS) reduction and morphological capillary changes around type IIa fibers.
evidence: This is supported by PECAM-1 immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Capillary changes caused by nNOS reduction may be associated with the mechanism of skeletal muscle degeneration and type IIa fiber reduction in BMD mice.
source: These results suggest that capillary changes caused by nNOS reduction may be associated with the mechanism of skeletal muscle degeneration and type IIa fiber reduction in BMD mice.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the observed correlations between nNOS reduction, capillary changes, and type IIa fiber loss.

claim: BMD mice may be useful in elucidating the pathomechanisms and developing vascular targeted therapies for human BMD.
source: BMD mice may be useful in elucidating the pathomechanisms and developing vascular targeted therapies for human BMD.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential utility of the mouse models.

claim: BMD is characterized by progressive muscle wasting and weakness.
source: Becker muscular dystrophy (BMD), an X-linked muscle disorder, is characterized by progressive muscle wasting and weakness, mostly caused by an in-frame variant in DMD encoding the sarcolemmal protein dystrophin.
evidence: This is established knowledge about BMD clinical features.

claim: BMD is mostly caused by an in-frame variant in DMD encoding the sarcolemmal protein dystrophin.
source: Becker muscular dystrophy (BMD), an X-linked muscle disorder, is characterized by progressive muscle wasting and weakness, mostly caused by an in-frame variant in DMD encoding the sarcolemmal protein dystrophin.
evidence: This is established knowledge about BMD molecular etiology.

claim: In BMD muscle tissues, truncated and reduced dystrophin is expressed.
source: In BMD muscle tissues, truncated and reduced dystrophin is expressed; therefore, its clinical status is generally milder than that of Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), an allelic disorder with complete loss of dystrophin (Koenig et al., 1989).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Koenig et al., 1989.

claim: BMD clinical status is generally milder than that of Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD).
source: In BMD muscle tissues, truncated and reduced dystrophin is expressed; therefore, its clinical status is generally milder than that of Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), an allelic disorder with complete loss of dystrophin (Koenig et al., 1989).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Koenig et al., 1989 and is established clinical knowledge.

claim: DMD is an allelic disorder with complete loss of dystrophin.
source: In BMD muscle tissues, truncated and reduced dystrophin is expressed; therefore, its clinical status is generally milder than that of Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), an allelic disorder with complete loss of dystrophin (Koenig et al., 1989).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Koenig et al., 1989.

claim: Some BMD affected individuals experience a near-normal lifestyle and lifespan, while others lose the ability to walk in their late teens or early 20s.
source: BMD is clinically heterogeneous, with some affected individuals experiencing a near-normal lifestyle and lifespan, while others lose the ability to walk in their late teens or early 20s (Beggs et al., 1991; Bushby and Gardner-Medwin, 1993; Comi et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Beggs et al., 1991; Bushby and Gardner-Medwin, 1993; Comi et al., 1994.

claim: A natural history study of patients with BMD revealed that part of the skeletal muscle phenotype may be associated with the genotype of DMD.
source: A natural history study of patients with BMD revealed that part of the skeletal muscle phenotype may be associated with the genotype of DMD and that there are several patterns of exon deletions associated with severe or milder phenotypes (Nakamura et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nakamura et al., 2023.

claim: There are several patterns of exon deletions associated with severe or milder phenotypes in BMD.
source: A natural history study of patients with BMD revealed that part of the skeletal muscle phenotype may be associated with the genotype of DMD and that there are several patterns of exon deletions associated with severe or milder phenotypes (Nakamura et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nakamura et al., 2023.

claim: In-frame exon deletions of BMD accumulate in exons 45–55 (first hotspot) or exons 3–7 (second hotspot) of DMD.
source: In-frame exon deletions of BMD accumulate in exons 45–55 (first hotspot) or exons 3–7 (second hotspot) of DMD.
evidence: This is established knowledge about BMD mutation patterns.

claim: 80% of all in-frame deletions were included in the first hotspot: exons 45–55.
source: Particularly, 80% of all in-frame deletions were included in the first hotspot: exons 45–55.
evidence: This is a statistical claim about BMD mutation distribution.

claim: The deletion of exons 45–47 (d45–47) is the most frequent, approximately 30% of patients with BMD have this in-frame deletion.
source: Among these, the deletion of exons 45–47 (d45–47) is the most frequent, approximately 30% of patients with BMD have this in-frame deletion.
evidence: This is a statistical claim about BMD mutation frequency.

claim: Deletion of exons 45–48 (d45–48) is the second most frequent; approximately 18% of patients with BMD have this deletion and a milder phenotype than D45–47.
source: Deletion of exons 45–48 (d45–48) is the second most frequent; approximately 18% of patients with BMD have this deletion and a milder phenotype than D45–47.
evidence: This is based on natural history study data, likely from Nakamura et al., 2023.

claim: The deletion of exons 45–49 (d45–49) has a more severe phenotype than D45–47.
source: In contrast, the deletion of exons 45–49 (d45–49) has a more severe phenotype than D45–47 (Nakamura et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nakamura et al., 2023.

claim: In the muscle tissue of patients with BMD, truncated dystrophin expression levels are lower than those of healthy controls.
source: In the muscle tissue of patients with BMD, truncated dystrophin expression levels are lower than those of healthy controls, and dystrophin immunohistochemistry shows a 'faint and patchy' staining pattern (Beggs et al., 1991; Jimi et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Beggs et al., 1991; Jimi et al., 1992.

claim: Dystrophin immunohistochemistry shows a 'faint and patchy' staining pattern in BMD muscle tissue.
source: In the muscle tissue of patients with BMD, truncated dystrophin expression levels are lower than those of healthy controls, and dystrophin immunohistochemistry shows a 'faint and patchy' staining pattern (Beggs et al., 1991; Jimi et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Beggs et al., 1991; Jimi et al., 1992.

claim: The truncated dystrophin expression levels in muscle tissues are well correlated with the clinical severity of BMD.
source: The correlation between the severity and expression levels of truncated dystrophin is still conflicting, and the truncated dystrophin expression levels in muscle tissues are well correlated with the clinical severity of BMD (Anthony et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Anthony et al., 2011.

claim: Truncated dystrophin levels do not appear to be a major determinant of disease severity in BMD.
source: However, there is another report that truncated dystrophin levels do not appear to be a major determinant of disease severity in BMD (van den Bergen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to van den Bergen et al., 2014.

claim: Dystrophin is a large filamentous protein with a molecular weight of 427 kDa.
source: Dystrophin is a large filamentous protein with a molecular weight of 427 kDa that protects the sarcolemma from mechanical stress during muscle contraction.
evidence: This is established knowledge about dystrophin structure.

claim: Dystrophin protects the sarcolemma from mechanical stress during muscle contraction.
source: Dystrophin is a large filamentous protein with a molecular weight of 427 kDa that protects the sarcolemma from mechanical stress during muscle contraction.
evidence: This is established knowledge about dystrophin function.

claim: Dystrophin connects to cytoskeletal protein families that can assemble into macromolecular structures with a large number of proteins and lipids.
source: Dystrophin connects to cytoskeletal protein families that can assemble into macromolecular structures with a large number of proteins and lipids (Le Rumeur et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Le Rumeur et al., 2010.

claim: BMD clinical heterogeneity is associated with the changes in dystrophin structure generated by exon deletion.
source: Recently, a report suggested that the BMD clinical heterogeneity is associated with the changes in dystrophin structure generated by exon deletion using an in silico prediction model (Nicolas et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nicolas et al., 2015.

claim: The d45–48 and d45–51 displayed a structure similar to that of wild-type (WT) dystrophin (hybrid repeat).
source: They expect that the d45–48 and d45–51 displayed a structure similar to that of wild-type (WT) dystrophin (hybrid repeat), whereas the d45–47 and d45–49 lead to proteins with an unrelated structure (fractional repeat) among the representative exon deletions in the BMD variant hotspot.
evidence: This is based on in silico predictions from Nicolas et al., 2015.

claim: The d45–47 and d45–49 lead to proteins with an unrelated structure (fractional repeat).
source: They expect that the d45–48 and d45–51 displayed a structure similar to that of wild-type (WT) dystrophin (hybrid repeat), whereas the d45–47 and d45–49 lead to proteins with an unrelated structure (fractional repeat) among the representative exon deletions in the BMD variant hotspot.
evidence: This is based on in silico predictions from Nicolas et al., 2015.

claim: Exon deletions associated with fractional repeats are expected to lead to a more severe BMD phenotype than those associated with hybrid repeats.
source: Exon deletions associated with fractional repeats are expected to lead to a more severe BMD phenotype than those associated with hybrid repeats; however, the influence of changes in dystrophin structure on clinical BMD severity is not fully understood.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on structural predictions.

claim: A BMD rat model carrying a deletion of exons 3–16 of the rat Dmd was generated using CRISPR/Cas9.
source: One group generated the first BMD rat model carrying a deletion of exons 3–16 of the rat Dmd using CRISPR/Cas9 (Teramoto et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Teramoto et al., 2020.

claim: The BMD rat model exhibited muscle degeneration, muscle fibrosis, heart fibrosis, and reduced truncated dystrophin levels.
source: This BMD rat model exhibited muscle degeneration, muscle fibrosis, heart fibrosis, and reduced truncated dystrophin levels.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Teramoto et al., 2020.

claim: A BMD mouse model carrying a deletion in exons 45–47 of the mouse Dmd was generated.
source: Another group generated a BMD mouse model carrying a deletion in exons 45–47 of the mouse Dmd (Heier et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Heier et al., 2023.

claim: The BMD mice show skeletal muscle weakness, heart dysfunction, increased myofiber size variability, increased centronuclear fibers, and reduced truncated dystrophin.
source: The BMD mice show skeletal muscle weakness, heart dysfunction, increased myofiber size variability, increased centronuclear fibers, and reduced truncated dystrophin.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Heier et al., 2023.

claim: Guide RNAs (gRNAs) were designed to target protospacer adjacent motif sequences upstream of Dmd exon 45 and downstream of Dmd exons 47, 48, and 49.
source: Guide RNAs (gRNAs) were designed to target protospacer adjacent motif sequences upstream of Dmd exon 45 and downstream of Dmd exons 47, 48, and 49.
evidence: This describes the experimental method used to generate the BMD mice.

claim: The genomic deletion of dystrophin exons 45–47, 45–48, and 45–49 was confirmed by cDNA sequencing.
source: We confirmed the genomic deletion of dystrophin exons 45–47, 45–48, and 45–49 by cDNA sequencing (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Double-strand breaks were formed inside the sequences corresponding to gRNAs in d45–48, d45–47, and d45–49 mice.
source: By analyzing the deletion breakpoint, we confirmed that double-strand breaks were formed inside the sequences corresponding to gRNAs in d45–48, d45–47, and d45–49 mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: d45–49 and mdx mice had large body weights at 1 and 3 months of age.
source: d45–49 and mdx mice had large body weights at 1 and 3 months of age, but the d45–48 and d45–47 mice did not differ from that in WT mice (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The d45–48 and d45–47 mice did not differ in body weight from WT mice at 1 and 3 months of age.
source: d45–49 and mdx mice had large body weights at 1 and 3 months of age, but the d45–48 and d45–47 mice did not differ from that in WT mice (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: At the age of 1 month, d45–47, d45–49, and mdx mice showed reduced forelimb grip strength compared to WT and d45–48 mice.
source: At the age of 1 month, d45–47, d45–49, and mdx mice showed reduced forelimb grip strength compared to WT and d45–48 mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The weakness of d45–47 mice was milder compared to d45–49 and mdx mice at 1 month of age.
source: However, the weakness of d45–47 mice was milder compared to d45–49, and mdx mice of the same age were used.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: At the age of 3 months, reduced grip strength in the d45–47 mice was remarkable, and d45–48 mice exhibited a slight reduction in forelimb grip strength.
source: At the age of 3 months, reduced grip strength in the d45–47 mice was remarkable, and d45–48 mice exhibited a slight reduction in forelimb grip strength.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: After 6 months, all three BMD mice reached the same levels of reduced forelimb grip strength, although not as much as that of mdx mice.
source: Finally, after 6 months, all three BMD mice reached the same levels of reduced forelimb grip strength, although not as much as that of mdx mice (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The hanging wire test showed reduced suspension times in the d45–49 and mdx mice.
source: The hanging wire test showed reduced suspension times in the d45–49 and mdx mice, although the WT, d45–48, and d45–47 mice exceeded the 600 s time limit (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: WT, d45–48, and d45–47 mice exceeded the 600 s time limit in the hanging wire test.
source: The hanging wire test showed reduced suspension times in the d45–49 and mdx mice, although the WT, d45–48, and d45–47 mice exceeded the 600 s time limit (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: WT, d45–48, and d45–47 mice could quickly bring their posterior legs up toward their faces and catch the wire during the hanging wire test.
source: Furthermore, the observation using video for the hanging wire test revealed changes in the mice moving during wire grasping: WT, d45–48, and d45–47 mice could quickly bring their posterior legs up toward their faces and catch the wire; in contrast, d45–49 and mdx mice could not raise their posterior legs above their chest (Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: This is supported by video observation data referenced as Figure 1—video 1.

claim: d45–49 and mdx mice could not raise their posterior legs above their chest during the hanging wire test.
source: Furthermore, the observation using video for the hanging wire test revealed changes in the mice moving during wire grasping: WT, d45–48, and d45–47 mice could quickly bring their posterior legs up toward their faces and catch the wire; in contrast, d45–49 and mdx mice could not raise their posterior legs above their chest (Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: This is supported by video observation data referenced as Figure 1—video 1.

claim: Opaque fibers increased at an earlier age of 1 month in d45–49 mice compared with WT mice.
source: Opaque fibers, which are thought to be precursors of necrotic fibers, increased at an earlier age of 1 month in d45–49 mice compared with WT mice; in contrast, the proportion of opaque fibers differs significantly between d45–47 and WT mice at 3 months, with an increased tendency only in 1-month-old mice (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The proportion of opaque fibers differs significantly between d45–47 and WT mice at 3 months, with an increased tendency only in 1-month-old mice.
source: Opaque fibers, which are thought to be precursors of necrotic fibers, increased at an earlier age of 1 month in d45–49 mice compared with WT mice; in contrast, the proportion of opaque fibers differs significantly between d45–47 and WT mice at 3 months, with an increased tendency only in 1-month-old mice (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Necrotic fibers were seen only in mdx mice at 1 month, but were also increased in d45–49 mice at 3 months.
source: Necrotic fibers were seen only in mdx mice at 1 month, but were also increased in d45–49 mice at 3 months (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Centronuclear fibers were increased in mdx mice and slightly increased in all BMD mice at 1 month.
source: Centronuclear fibers, which are thought to be regenerated fibers after muscle damage, were increased in mdx mice and slightly increased in all BMD mice at 1 month.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: At 3 months, centronuclear fibers were increased in the d45–49 mice.
source: At 3 months, centronuclear fibers were increased in the d45–49 mice (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: At 1 month, an increased fibrotic area was seen only in mdx mice.
source: At 1 month, an increased fibrotic area was seen only in mdx mice, but after 3 months, it was seen also in d45–49 mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: After 3 months, increased fibrotic area was seen in d45–49 mice.
source: At 1 month, an increased fibrotic area was seen only in mdx mice, but after 3 months, it was seen also in d45–49 mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: After 6 months, fibrosis gradually became apparent, even in d45–48 and d45–47 mice.
source: After 6 months, fibrosis gradually became apparent, even in d45–48 and d45–47 mice (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: All BMD mice exhibited increased centronuclear fibers and fibrosis in the diaphragm muscles at 12 months.
source: HE and Sirius Red staining revealed increased centronuclear fibers and fibrosis in the diaphragm muscles, and increased myocardial fibrosis in the cardiac muscles in all BMD mice at 12 months (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: All BMD mice exhibited increased myocardial fibrosis in the cardiac muscles at 12 months.
source: HE and Sirius Red staining revealed increased centronuclear fibers and fibrosis in the diaphragm muscles, and increased myocardial fibrosis in the cardiac muscles in all BMD mice at 12 months (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: The changes in diaphragm and cardiac muscles in BMD mice were minor compared with those observed in mdx mice.
source: However, these changes were minor compared with those observed in mdx mice.
evidence: This is based on comparison of histological data between BMD and mdx mice.

claim: Muscle degeneration and fibrosis deteriorated in the following order: d45–49, d45–47, and d45–48 mice.
source: All BMD mice exhibited muscle degeneration and fibrosis; however, these findings became more apparent with exon deletions: the time-course histopathological observations revealed that muscle degeneration and fibrosis deteriorated in the following order: d45–49, d45–47, and d45–48 mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by time-course histopathological data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Dystrophin immunohistochemistry demonstrated a reduction of dystrophin and 'faint' and 'patchy' staining patterns in all BMD mice.
source: Dystrophin immunohistochemistry demonstrated a reduction of dystrophin and 'faint' and 'patchy' staining patterns in all BMD mice.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: All BMD mice showed decreased levels of nNOS expression in the sarcolemma to levels similar to mdx mice.
source: Consistent with the lack of an nNOS-binding site, encoded by exons 42–45, all BMD mice showed decreased levels of nNOS expression in the sarcolemma to levels similar to mdx mice.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry and Western blot data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The expression of aSG was detected on the sarcolemma in all BMD mice, whereas the expression levels were slightly low compared with WT mice.
source: On the contrary, consistent with the remaining dystroglycan-binding site: encoded by exons 63–70, the expression of aSG was detected on the sarcolemma in all BMD mice, whereas the expression levels were slightly low compared with WT mice (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Western blot analysis demonstrated truncated dystrophin expression in all BMD mice at 1 and 3 months.
source: Western blot (WB) analysis demonstrated truncated dystrophin expression in all BMD mice at 1 and 3 months (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The truncated dystrophin expression levels were reduced to 30–40% at 1 month, and 10–20% at 3 months compared to those in WT mice.
source: The truncated dystrophin expression levels were reduced to 30–40% at 1 month, and 10–20% at 3 months compared to those in WT mice (Figure 3E), despite adequate levels of dystrophin mRNA expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot quantification shown in Figure 3E and mRNA data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: BMD mice had adequate levels of dystrophin mRNA expression.
source: The truncated dystrophin expression levels were reduced to 30–40% at 1 month, and 10–20% at 3 months compared to those in WT mice (Figure 3E), despite adequate levels of dystrophin mRNA expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The utrophin expression levels showed only an increased tendency in all BMD mice at 3 months.
source: By WB analysis, the utrophin expression levels showed only an increased tendency in all BMD mice at 3 months, whereas there was a significant increase in mdx mice (8-fold at 1 month and 30-fold at 3 months) compared to WT mice (Figure 3C, F).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3C, F.

claim: There was a significant increase in utrophin in mdx mice (8-fold at 1 month and 30-fold at 3 months) compared to WT mice.
source: By WB analysis, the utrophin expression levels showed only an increased tendency in all BMD mice at 3 months, whereas there was a significant increase in mdx mice (8-fold at 1 month and 30-fold at 3 months) compared to WT mice (Figure 3C, F).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3C, F.

claim: Utrophin mRNA expression levels did not differ among WT, BMD, and mdx mice.
source: In contrast, utrophin mRNA expression levels did not differ among WT, BMD, and mdx mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Western blot analysis demonstrated decreased levels of nNOS in all BMD mice as well as mdx mice at 3 months.
source: Further, WB analysis demonstrated decreased levels of nNOS in all BMD mice as well as mdx mice at 3 months (Figure 3D, G), despite adequate levels of nNOS mRNA expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3D, G.

claim: BMD mice had adequate levels of nNOS mRNA expression.
source: Further, WB analysis demonstrated decreased levels of nNOS in all BMD mice as well as mdx mice at 3 months (Figure 3D, G), despite adequate levels of nNOS mRNA expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Patients with muscle diseases, including BMD, show changes in MRI or CT images of a particular group of muscles.
source: Generally, patients with muscle diseases, including BMD, show changes in MRI or CT images of a particular group of muscles (Díaz-Manera et al., 2015; Tasca et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Díaz-Manera et al., 2015; Tasca et al., 2012.

claim: mdx mice showed diffuse muscle degeneration on HE staining and no remarkable histopathological differences between the inner and outer part of the TA.
source: mdx mice showed diffuse muscle degeneration on HE staining and no remarkable histopathological differences between the inner and outer part of the TA.
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: BMD mice showed significant site-specific muscle degeneration in the inner part of the TA compared with the outer part.
source: In contrast, BMD mice showed significant site-specific muscle degeneration in the inner part of the TA compared with the outer part (Figure 4A, upper panel).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: d45–49 mice showed site-specific muscle degeneration predominantly in the RF, VM, VI, MF, and LG, whereas less muscle degeneration was observed in the VL and IC.
source: Even in the quadriceps and erector spinae, d45–49 mice showed site-specific muscle degeneration predominantly in the RF, VM, VI, MF, and LG, whereas less muscle degeneration was observed in the VL and IC.
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 4D, G.

claim: mdx mice exhibited diffuse muscle generation in all parts of the quadriceps and erector spinae.
source: In contrast, mdx mice exhibited diffuse muscle generation in all parts of the quadriceps and erector spinae (Figure 4D, G).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 4D, G.

claim: Serum creatine kinase (CK) levels were high in mdx mice, and were two- to fourfold higher in all BMD mice after 3 months compared to WT mice.
source: Serum creatine kinase (CK) levels at 1, 3, 6, and 12 months were high in mdx mice, and were two- to fourfold higher in all BMD mice after 3 months compared to WT mice, although the difference was not statistically significant (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by serum CK measurement data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In WT mice at 3 months, type IIb fibers were dominant in the outer part of the TA, while type IIa and IIx fibers were dominant in the inner part of the TA.
source: In WT mice at 3 months, type IIb fibers were dominant in the outer part of the TA, while type IIa and IIx fibers were dominant in the inner part of the TA, although type I fibers were rare in the TA (Figure 4A, middle and lower panels).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Type I fibers were rare in the TA of WT mice.
source: In WT mice at 3 months, type IIb fibers were dominant in the outer part of the TA, while type IIa and IIx fibers were dominant in the inner part of the TA, although type I fibers were rare in the TA (Figure 4A, middle and lower panels).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The ratio of type IIa fibers in the inner part of the TA was decreased in all BMD and mdx mice compared with WT mice.
source: These deviations in muscle fiber type in the TA were also seen in BMD and mdx mice at 3 months, however, the ratio of type IIa fibers in the inner part of the TA was decreased in all BMD and mdx mice compared with WT mice.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4B, C.

claim: The ratio of type IIb to type IIx fibers was unchanged in all BMD and mdx mice compared with that in WT mice.
source: In contrast, the ratio of type IIb to type IIx fibers was unchanged in all BMD and mdx mice compared with that in WT mice (Figure 4B, C).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4B, C.

claim: Type IIb fibers were present dominantly in the VL and outer part of the RF and IC in WT mice at 3 months.
source: The deviation in muscle fiber type was seen even in the quadriceps and erector spinae in WT mice at 3 months: type IIb fibers were present dominantly in the VL and outer part of the RF and IC, and type IIa fibers were present dominantly in the inner part of the RF, VM, VI, MF, and LG.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4E, H.

claim: Type IIa fibers were present dominantly in the inner part of the RF, VM, VI, MF, and LG in WT mice at 3 months.
source: The deviation in muscle fiber type was seen even in the quadriceps and erector spinae in WT mice at 3 months: type IIb fibers were present dominantly in the VL and outer part of the RF and IC, and type IIa fibers were present dominantly in the inner part of the RF, VM, VI, MF, and LG.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4E, H.

claim: Type I fibers were present in the VI, MF, and LG in WT mice at 3 months.
source: Type I fibers, which are rare in the TA, were present in the VI, MF, and LG.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4E, H.

claim: The VL and IC were mostly composed of type IIb fibers and rarely contained other fiber types in WT mice.
source: In particular, the VL and IC were mostly composed of type IIb fibers and rarely contained other fiber types (Figure 4E, H).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4E, H.

claim: The ratio of type IIa fibers in the inner part of the RF, VM, VI, MF, and LG was lower in all BMD and mdx mice than in WT mice at 3 months.
source: In contrast, all BMD and mdx mice showed the same fiber type deviation in the quadriceps and erector spinae at 3 months, however, the ratio of type IIa fibers in the inner part of the RF, VM, VI, MF, and LG was lower than that in WT mice.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4F, I.

claim: The ratio of type I and IIb fibers was unchanged or slightly increased in all BMD and mdx mice compared to that in WT mice.
source: In contrast, the ratio of type I and IIb fibers was unchanged or slightly increased in all BMD and mdx mice compared to that in WT mice (Figure 4F, I).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4F, I.

claim: The cross-sectional areas (CSAs) of TA muscles in BMD and mdx mice were rather high at 3 months compared with those of WT mice.
source: We examined the cross-sectional areas (CSAs) of TA muscles in BMD and mdx mice to evaluate the association between type IIa fiber reduction and muscle atrophy. Their CSAs were rather high at 3 months, in accordance with muscle hypertrophy, compared with those of WT mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by CSA measurement data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Murf1 and atrogin-1 mRNA expression levels did not differ among WT, BMD, and mdx mice.
source: In addition, Murf1 and atrogin-1 mRNA expression levels (representative muscle atrophy inducing factors) did not differ among WT, BMD, and mdx mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: The composition of muscle fiber types changes according to postnatal development in mice.
source: The composition of muscle fiber types changes according to postnatal development in mice (Miwa et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Miwa et al., 2009.

claim: In WT mice, the count of type IIa fibers was approximately 100 fibers in a TA section at 1 month, and were twofold increased at 3 and 6 months, then was slightly down-regulated at 12 months.
source: In WT mice, the count of type IIa fibers was approximately 100 fibers in a TA section at 1 month, and were twofold increased at 3 and 6 months, then was slightly down-regulated at 12 months.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5A, B.

claim: The count of type IIa fibers in BMD mice was the same as that in WT mice at 1 month but decreased after 3 months.
source: In contrast, the count of type IIa fibers in BMD mice was the same as that in WT mice at 1 month but decreased after 3 months, which is opposite to that of WT mice.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5A, B.

claim: In mdx mice, the number of type IIa fibers was low at 1 month and did not recover throughout the observation period.
source: Furthermore, in mdx mice, the number of type IIa fibers was low at 1 month and did not recover throughout the observation period (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: There is a report about a shift in the muscle fiber type composition in a cardiotoxin (CTX)-induced regeneration model in the TA of WT mice, which suggested the vulnerability of type IIa fibers to CTX injection.
source: Although the mechanisms of type IIa fiber reduction in BMD mice remain unclear, there is a report about a shift in the muscle fiber type composition in a cardiotoxin (CTX)-induced regeneration model in the TA of WT mice, which suggested the vulnerability of type IIa fibers to CTX injection (Dalle et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dalle et al., 2020.

claim: On days 5 and 7 after CTX injection, only type IIb fibers appeared, with the recovery of regenerated muscle fibers.
source: On days 5 and 7 after CTX injection, only type IIb fibers appeared, with the recovery of regenerated muscle fibers.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The recovery of type IIa and IIx fibers was delayed compared to that of type IIb fibers: days 14 and 28 after CTX injection in type IIa and IIx fibers, respectively.
source: The recovery of type IIa and IIx fibers was delayed compared to that of type IIb fibers: days 14 and 28 after CTX injection in type IIa and IIx fibers, respectively (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, middle and right panels).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Vascular dysfunction accompanied by sarcolemmal nNOS reduction is hypothesized to be involved in the pathomechanisms of muscle impairment in human DMD.
source: It is hypothesized that vascular dysfunction accompanied by sarcolemmal nNOS reduction is involved in the pathomechanisms of muscle impairment in human DMD (Miike et al., 1987; Thomas et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Miike et al., 1987; Thomas et al., 1998.

claim: WT mice showed 'ring-pattern' capillaries contacting type IIa and IIx fibers at the inner part of TA.
source: WT mice showed 'ring-pattern' capillaries contacting type IIa and IIx fibers at the inner part of TA.
evidence: This is supported by PECAM-1 immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Capillaries contacting type IIa and IIx fibers showed morphological changes to 'dot-pattern' at the inner part of TA in d45–49 and mdx mice.
source: On the contrary, capillaries contacting type IIa and IIx fibers showed morphological changes to 'dot-pattern' at the inner part of TA in d45–49 and mdx mice (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by PECAM-1 immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Capillaries that circumferentially contact muscle fibers were rich in WT mice, and showed remarkable 'ring-pattern' around type IIa fibers.
source: Especially in type IIa fibers, capillaries that circumferentially contact muscle fibers were rich in WT mice, and showed remarkable 'ring-pattern' around type IIa fibers in WT mice.
evidence: This is supported by PECAM-1 immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Around type IIx fibers in WT mice, capillaries contacting muscle fibers were poor compared with those of type IIa fibers, with 'incomplete ring-patterns'.
source: In contrast, around type IIx fibers in WT mice, capillaries contacting muscle fibers were poor compared with those of type IIa fibers, with 'incomplete ring-patterns' around type IIx fibers in WT mice.
evidence: This is supported by PECAM-1 immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: In d45–49 and mdx mice, circumferentially contacting capillaries were reduced around the type IIa and IIx fibers, and changed to a 'dot-pattern'.
source: In d45–49 and mdx mice, these circumferentially contacting capillaries were reduced around the type IIa and IIx fibers, and changed to a 'dot-pattern'.
evidence: This is supported by PECAM-1 immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Capillaries contacting around type IIb and I fibers showed a 'dot-pattern' even in WT mice.
source: Capillaries contacting around type IIb and I fibers showed a 'dot-pattern' even in WT mice (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by PECAM-1 immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The endothelial area in contact with both type IIa and IIx fibers were decreased in d45–49 and mdx mice compared with WT mice.
source: According to these morphological capillary changes, the endothelial area in contact with both type IIa and IIx fibers were decreased in d45–49 and mdx mice compared with WT mice.
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The reduction rate of endothelial area around type IIa fibers (60%) was larger than that around type IIx fibers (35%).
source: The reduction rate around type IIa fibers (60%) was larger than that around type IIx fibers (35%), reflecting the difference between the 'ring-pattern' around type IIa fibers and the 'incomplete ring-pattern' around type IIx fibers in WT mice (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: There were fewer interconnected capillaries in BMD and mdx mice than in WT mice.
source: We confirmed that there were fewer interconnected capillaries in BMD and mdx mice than in WT mice (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by PECAM-1 immunohistochemistry data on longitudinal sections shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The severity of BMD in mice might be influenced by the qualitative shift in truncated dystrophin proteins along with exon deletions, and not by quantitative changes.
source: We confirmed decreased levels of truncated dystrophin in all BMD mice; however, the expression levels were almost the same despite differences in phenotypic severity. Therefore, the severity of BMD in mice might be influenced by the qualitative shift in truncated dystrophin proteins along with exon deletions, and not by quantitative changes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that dystrophin levels were similar across BMD mice with different severities.

claim: In-frame exon deletions possibly induce a structural shift in dystrophin, and the collapse of the dystrophin structure might influence BMD severity.
source: Indeed, using an in silico prediction model, it has been reported that in-frame exon deletions possibly induce a structural shift in dystrophin, and the collapse of the dystrophin structure might influence BMD severity (Nicolas et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nicolas et al., 2015.

claim: Muscles located near the body surface are rich in white muscle fibers, while the deep muscles are rich in medium and red muscle fibers.
source: It has been known that muscles located near the body surface are rich in white muscle fibers, while the deep muscles are rich in medium and red muscle fibers (Ogata, 1958).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ogata, 1958.

claim: Type IIa fibers are also known as fast-oxidative fibers.
source: Type IIa fibers are also known as fast-oxidative fibers (Talbot and Maves, 2016) and are known to have fatigue resistance compared with type IIb and IIx fibers, known as having the least and the second least fatigue-resistant fibers (Larsson et al., 1991) type IIa fiber reduction is thought to contribute to muscle fatigability (Percival et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Talbot and Maves, 2016.

claim: Type IIa fibers have fatigue resistance compared with type IIb and IIx fibers.
source: Type IIa fibers are also known as fast-oxidative fibers (Talbot and Maves, 2016) and are known to have fatigue resistance compared with type IIb and IIx fibers, known as having the least and the second least fatigue-resistant fibers (Larsson et al., 1991) type IIa fiber reduction is thought to contribute to muscle fatigability (Percival et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Larsson et al., 1991.

claim: Type IIa fiber reduction is thought to contribute to muscle fatigability.
source: Type IIa fibers are also known as fast-oxidative fibers (Talbot and Maves, 2016) and are known to have fatigue resistance compared with type IIb and IIx fibers, known as having the least and the second least fatigue-resistant fibers (Larsson et al., 1991) type IIa fiber reduction is thought to contribute to muscle fatigability (Percival et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Percival et al., 2010.

claim: Mice lacking the RNA-binding protein Musashi-2, which is predominantly expressed in slow-type muscle fibers, showed a reduction in type IIa fibers along with reduced muscle contraction force.
source: Recently, it was reported that mice lacking the RNA-binding protein Musashi-2, which is predominantly expressed in slow-type muscle fibers, showed a reduction in type IIa fibers along with reduced muscle contraction force (Furuichi et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Furuichi et al., 2023.

claim: Decrease in type IIa fibers contributes to the muscle weakness and fatigability in BMD mice.
source: These findings suggest that decrease in type IIa fibers contributes to the muscle weakness and fatigability in BMD mice.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed correlation between type IIa fiber reduction and muscle weakness.

claim: Only type I, IIa, and IIx fibers are present in human skeletal muscle, and type IIb fibers appear to be absent.
source: In addition, only type I, IIa, and IIx fibers are present in human skeletal muscle, and type IIb fibers appear to be absent (Talbot and Maves, 2016; Schiaffino and Reggiani, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Talbot and Maves, 2016; Schiaffino and Reggiani, 2011.

claim: The reduction of type IIa fibers might have a greater effect on the skeletal muscle function of human BMD than that of BMD mice.
source: Thus, the reduction of type IIa fibers might have a greater effect on the skeletal muscle function of human BMD than that of BMD mice.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the difference in fiber type composition between humans and mice.

claim: A decrease in type IIa fibers was observed in microgravity-induced muscle atrophy in WT mice, where a decrease in sarcolemmal nNOS occurred.
source: A decrease in type IIa fibers was also observed in microgravity-induced muscle atrophy in WT mice, where a decrease in sarcolemmal nNOS occurred (Sandonà et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sandonà et al., 2012.

claim: The expression level of nNOS is higher in type IIa fibers than in type I and IIb fibers.
source: It has been reported that the expression level of nNOS is higher in type IIa fibers than in type I and IIb fibers (Planitzer et al., 2001) and that nNOS-deficient mice have reduced type IIa fibers compared to WT mice (Percival et al., 2010) and reduced capillary density only in the inner part of the muscle (Baum et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Planitzer et al., 2001.

claim: nNOS-deficient mice have reduced type IIa fibers compared to WT mice.
source: It has been reported that the expression level of nNOS is higher in type IIa fibers than in type I and IIb fibers (Planitzer et al., 2001) and that nNOS-deficient mice have reduced type IIa fibers compared to WT mice (Percival et al., 2010) and reduced capillary density only in the inner part of the muscle (Baum et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Percival et al., 2010.

claim: nNOS-deficient mice have reduced capillary density only in the inner part of the muscle.
source: It has been reported that the expression level of nNOS is higher in type IIa fibers than in type I and IIb fibers (Planitzer et al., 2001) and that nNOS-deficient mice have reduced type IIa fibers compared to WT mice (Percival et al., 2010) and reduced capillary density only in the inner part of the muscle (Baum et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Baum et al., 2023.

claim: BMD mice showed morphological capillary changes from a 'ring-pattern' to a 'dot-pattern' with decreased nNOS expression in the sarcolemma and fewer capillaries in circumferential contact with type IIa fibers.
source: By examining BMD mice, we found for the first time morphological capillary changes from a 'ring-pattern' to a 'dot-pattern' with decreased nNOS expression in the sarcolemma and fewer capillaries in circumferential contact with type IIa fibers.
evidence: This is a novel finding from the current study supported by PECAM-1 immunohistochemistry data.

claim: Type IIa fibers may require numerous capillaries and maintained blood flow, compared with other muscle fibers.
source: These results suggest that type IIa fibers may require numerous capillaries and maintained blood flow, compared with other muscle fibers, and this high requirement for blood flow might be associated with the type IIa fiber-specific decay in BMD mice.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the observed capillary patterns around different fiber types.

claim: The high requirement for blood flow in type IIa fibers might be associated with the type IIa fiber-specific decay in BMD mice.
source: These results suggest that type IIa fibers may require numerous capillaries and maintained blood flow, compared with other muscle fibers, and this high requirement for blood flow might be associated with the type IIa fiber-specific decay in BMD mice.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the observed correlations.

claim: Between the main muscle capillaries running parallel to the muscle fibers, there are transversely interconnected branches and capillary loops.
source: Between the main muscle capillaries running parallel to the muscle fibers, there are transversely interconnected branches and capillary loops (Haas and Nwadozi, 2015), and the capillary changes in BMD mice may be associated with the deterioration of these interconnected branches and capillary loops (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Haas and Nwadozi, 2015.

claim: The capillary changes in BMD mice may be associated with the deterioration of interconnected branches and capillary loops.
source: Between the main muscle capillaries running parallel to the muscle fibers, there are transversely interconnected branches and capillary loops (Haas and Nwadozi, 2015), and the capillary changes in BMD mice may be associated with the deterioration of these interconnected branches and capillary loops (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the observed capillary changes.

claim: Vascular dysfunction has been implicated in muscle damage in canine model of DMD.
source: Vascular dysfunction has been implicated in muscle damage in canine model of DMD (Kodippili et al., 2021) and in human DMD (Thomas et al., 1998), and our analysis of BMD mice also suggests that the reduction of type IIa fibers may be influenced by vascular dysfunction with reduced sarcolemmal nNOS as well as fragility and delayed recovery.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kodippili et al., 2021.

claim: Vascular dysfunction has been implicated in muscle damage in human DMD.
source: Vascular dysfunction has been implicated in muscle damage in canine model of DMD (Kodippili et al., 2021) and in human DMD (Thomas et al., 1998), and our analysis of BMD mice also suggests that the reduction of type IIa fibers may be influenced by vascular dysfunction with reduced sarcolemmal nNOS as well as fragility and delayed recovery.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Thomas et al., 1998.

claim: The reduction of type IIa fibers may be influenced by vascular dysfunction with reduced sarcolemmal nNOS as well as fragility and delayed recovery.
source: Vascular dysfunction has been implicated in muscle damage in canine model of DMD (Kodippili et al., 2021) and in human DMD (Thomas et al., 1998), and our analysis of BMD mice also suggests that the reduction of type IIa fibers may be influenced by vascular dysfunction with reduced sarcolemmal nNOS as well as fragility and delayed recovery.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the observed correlations in BMD mice.
